rv.q: The lovers, outcasts and locals who wander through Arden tip winks to its composer pianist, Michael Bruce, and will him to “shut up” or to play on cue. That mime is part of a grander concept behind director Josie Rourke’s delicate and delightful production, which finds a perfect balance between West End spectacle and Shakespearean purity.

All this to a lyrical piano backing on-stage by Michael Bruce, a charming presence. The gently comic untangling of the daisy-chain of lovers - from a shy shepherd and his scornful paramour to Rosalind and Alfred Enoch’s decent Orlando - and happy ending are truly touching and make you feel (if briefly), as in Shakespeare’s song, that life is ind...
But this is a joyous staging, and its rich diversity of casting embraces the spirit of both the play and this new venue.
Rourke's production sacrifices a certain amount of clarity for in-the-moment entertainment. But I think that's forgivable, especially when it looks and sounds as good as this.
Rourke won't let the play's magic talk for itself.
But, in the end, it's Bruce's hypnotic score that clinches the play's uneven pleasures.
Leah Harvey is a fresh and candid Rosalind; Alfred Enoch injects vigour into the often limp Orlando (though he overeggs the humour of his woodland verses).
Josie Rourke's staging of As It demonstrates just how well suited this hip and happening upstart is to classical-theatrical revels.
Not a staging to lose your heart to, then; but its sunny intervals offer welcome warmth on a cold night.
This is a layered, delicate production that's as detailed in its visuals as it is in the poignancy of its reflections and nuance of its comedy.
Inside @sohoplace, there is warmth and laughter.

A new theatre presents an old classic with a modern and fresh take, the inclusion of music and BSL makes for a terrifically accessible As It, while some incredible performances make this an enchanting watch.
Plenty to enjoy here, then. But it doesn't entirely cohere as a whole.
Whether you've seen As It a hundred times or never, there's much pleasure and delight to be had.
But there is a lot of pleasure to be found in its pell-mell rush to entertain.

Josie Rourke has an eye for fun and in this comfortable theatre with its good sight-lines and fine acoustics, where no audience member is very far from the action, there is a good chance everyone can enjoy that fun.
